title: Push-button verifying compilation for practical systems

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a toolchain that turns practical systems code and a stated functional specification into an executable accompanied by a machine-checked proof that it meets that specification. Developers would describe both the implementation and its required behavior; the toolchain would automatically discharge the resulting proof obligations and connect the proof to the emitted binary. Functional correctness here means implementing the specified behavior, rather than establishing only a narrower property such as memory safety or crash freedom. The underlying verifying-compiler idea includes generating verification conditions from programs, specifications and a programming methodology.

Proposed scope: a useful language and execution envelope capable of expressing systems such as operating-system services, compilers, databases and networked services, with total development effort comparable to ordinary development. The distinctive combination is rich functional assurance, automatic proof production, executable-level coverage and sustainable cost. A tool that conservatively rejects difficult programs can remain sound, but successful compilation of representative practical systems is essential to this proposal. It does not require an algorithm that decides every property of every possible program.

significance.text: Much software assurance relies on reviews and tests, although some systems already have machine-checked correctness proofs. If the proposed automation, scope and cost were achieved, specification-relative assurance could become a routine compilation result. For properties actually proved, violations would be ruled out throughout the supported execution model under the stated assumptions, rather than merely remaining undiscovered by testing. seL4’s binary-correctness statements illustrate this relationship between a specification and an executable for configurations supporting that proof.

Conditional downstream synthesis: making such assurance affordable to ordinary teams could extend strong correctness guarantees beyond exceptional verification projects. Teams could spend less effort searching for violations already excluded by proof and more effort reviewing requirements, interfaces and environmental assumptions. Wider adoption could improve confidence in infrastructure assembled from verified components, but adoption, composition across organizations and inexpensive maintenance would require additional capabilities and evidence.

The guarantee would remain conditional. A proof can establish faithful implementation of an inadequate specification; it cannot by itself show that the specification captures user intent. Hardware behavior, instruction-set and operating-environment models, trusted checking components and the underlying logic also bound what follows in physical execution. seL4 explicitly identifies hardware faults and unexpected memory changes as circumstances outside its correctness predictions. Consequently, the proposed advance would not establish unconditional freedom from every kind of failure.

The comparison with an ordinary compiler concerns workflow: assurance would become a required toolchain output. Proof search has limits that ordinary translation does not remove. General semantic questions are undecidable, so a useful verifier must operate within a declared envelope and may fail to establish a true property. The transformative claim is therefore practical breadth and affordability, not a universal correctness decision procedure.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability combines expressive systems programming with automatic discharge of rich functional proof obligations at an ordinary development burden. Existing evidence shows substantial proof engineering and increasingly capable automation, rather than a simple divide between manual proofs and fully automatic verification. Verus, for example, combines general semi-automated techniques with full automation for restricted cases. The challenge is to broaden successful automation without weakening the properties established or requiring specialist intervention whenever a program becomes difficult.

Engineering synthesis: proof generation must handle the invariants, abstraction boundaries and interactions that practical systems create, including concurrency and specified failure behavior. It must also connect source-level reasoning through compilation to the actual executable. These are distinct obligations: proving that a compiler preserves source semantics does not establish that the source satisfies its application specification, while proving a source program correct leaves a gap unless translation and execution assumptions are covered. Success must combine these links within a manageable trusted base.

The remaining practical barriers include non-expert usability, predictable proof-search cost, understandable feedback when verification fails and the effort required to express specifications and supporting invariants. DARPA PROVERS explicitly targets accessibility for traditional developers and reduced proof-repair workload. Restricted autonomous binary proofs reported in October 2026 show why it would be too broad to claim that interactive annotation dominates every relevant verification task. The supplied evidence neither demonstrates the complete proposed combination nor establishes its exhaustive absence as of 1 November 2026.

current_state.text: Leino and Schulte’s 2006 verifying-compiler text describes establishing source-program correctness before compilation, using automatically generated verification conditions derived from programs, specifications and a programming methodology. The supplied review had access to the introduction, although the retained extraction was truncated later in the document. The research also attributes the grand-challenge formulation to C. A. R. Hoare’s January 2003 JACM article, but no retained Hoare artifact was available to verify its exact wording or bibliographic attribution. The executable-proof and cost requirements in this record are explicit extensions of the historical goal.

seL4 demonstrates functional correctness for verified kernel configurations and binary correctness for configurations supporting that additional property. Its project proofs page reports no functional-correctness defects in verified code since completion of the 2009 proof, while acknowledging that user expectations may be absent from the specification and that unverified parts can contain defects. This is a substantial project-reported achievement with configuration-specific scope; the supplied evidence does not establish a comparative ranking among deployed kernels.

Historical seL4 project statistics place design, documentation, implementation and verification at approximately 25 person-years through first proof completion in 2009, including research, tools and libraries. Anthropic’s 22 October 2026 article separately reports approximately two person-years of implementation and 20 of verification, citing the verification work. These figures have different accounting scopes and should not be treated as present-day marginal verification costs. The research additionally reports approximately 10,000 source lines for the verified 64-bit RISC-V kernel as of April 2025 and ongoing multicore verification. Those two FAQ-specific assertions remain unconfirmed because the supplied review found the retained FAQ extraction unreadable.

CompCert’s documentation identifies version 3.18, dated 31 August 2026, and describes verified compilation from a large subset of C to assembly. Its semantic-preservation result can carry separately established source-level correctness through compilation; it does not itself prove that an arbitrary source program meets an application specification. Preservation must also be read with its treatment of undefined behavior and permitted nondeterminism: it is inaccurate to say that every incorrect source behavior must be preserved, since compilation can eliminate behaviors classified as going wrong.

The SOSP 2024 Verus paper, DOI 10.1145/3694715.3695952, reports case studies totaling 6.1K implementation lines and 31K proof lines. It reports faster verification and reduced developer effort in its evaluated comparisons, combining general semi-automation with full proof automation for special cases. Those results demonstrate progress in systems verification, while retaining substantial proof content and trusting the verifier, solvers and Rust compiler. They do not establish general automatic functional verification of emitted binaries at the proposed cost.

The research describes IronFleet, attributed to SOSP 2015, as proving safety and liveness for a Paxos-based replicated state machine and a sharded store while requiring substantial developer assistance. The supplied review could inspect only a GitHub viewer shell, rather than the paper. These paper-specific findings and the reported assistance characterization therefore remain unverified in this record; no evaluation line counts or verified DOI are asserted. This access limitation does not establish that the reported results are false.

On 22 October 2026, Anthropic and Theorem reported Claude-produced, Rocq-checked no-crash proofs for 239 entry points across 123 OSS-Fuzz libraries. The demonstrations concern single-threaded static RISC-V binaries executing as modeled Linux processes with fixed memory budgets. The appendix specifies inputs under 64 MiB, refining the article’s looser 64 MB wording. The reported successful proofs total approximately 180 million lines, with typical proofs around 600,000 lines and a median binary length of approximately 18,000 instructions. These are attributed results from the article and appendix; the proof corpus was not independently checked in the supplied review.

The October 2026 result establishes narrower properties than full functional correctness. Crash freedom does not establish termination, and coverage of selected entry points does not imply that entire libraries contain no bugs. The appendix explains limitations of the behavioral equivalence used in the development, including its treatment of crashes and nontermination, alongside the additional no-crash theorem. The article describes releasing trusted components, complete proofs for tests requiring no patch and specifications for tests it could not prove. That release description should not be read as independently checked access to every reported proof.

Proofcraft reported on 2 September 2025 that seL4’s proofs covered all Arm platforms then supported by the kernel, including a newly added 23rd platform requiring no additional proof work. This is evidence of proof reuse across platform additions for one kernel. It does not establish unrestricted configuration coverage, multicore verification or a general-purpose verifying compiler.

DARPA describes PROVERS as a 42-month, three-phase program pursuing non-expert usability and reduced proof-repair effort. Its account credits PEARLS with demonstrations of AI support and automation for proof generation and maintenance. The completed PEARLS page is an unmaintained historical description; program completion alone does not show that its full ambitions, or this record’s target, were achieved. NSF’s Software and Hardware Foundations synopsis under NSF 25-543 funds work including analysis, synthesis, compositionality, verifiability and adaptability. It describes research scope rather than a completed toolchain.

The research cites Brun and colleagues’ September 2026 roadmap as treating automatic proof synthesis and its integration with other capabilities as open challenges. The supplied review had no readable retained roadmap text: the ACM PDF was unavailable and the author bibliography capture contained an error message. That particular characterization remains unconfirmed. More broadly, the supplied material contains no bounded freshness search establishing the complete state of the field on 1 November 2026. Its dated achievements remain informative without proving either availability or absence of the full proposed capability.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: a team without specialist formal-methods expertise develops a concurrent multicore operating-system service, a small compiler or a replicated store in the supported language, together with an independently reviewable external functional specification. The successful demonstration must emit a working binary and a machine-checked proof that it refines that specification, including crash and recovery behavior where specified. A tool that rejects every submission would not satisfy this criterion.
completion_criteria.label: Non-specialists' working binary machine-checked to refine external functional specification

completion_criteria.text: Proposed verification contract: the toolchain must withhold certified output when it cannot discharge the obligations, while distinguishing failure to find a proof from a demonstrated specification violation. The evaluation should identify which functional properties were established, whether termination or liveness was included and which concurrency, failure and environmental behaviors were modeled. The emitted proof must be demonstrably connected to the exact executable being evaluated.
completion_criteria.label: Executable-bound certification withheld for undischarged obligations, distinct from violations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed cost criterion: total additional specification and verification effort should be on the order of writing and testing the system once. Reporting should include human effort, computation, specialist assistance and work performed outside the nominal development team, so that automation does not merely conceal displaced labor. This is a proposed threshold, not an established standard; it imposes neither an hour-count limit nor an all-bug-classes requirement. Keeping assurance costs proportional across later changes is a separate target associated with SWE-05.
completion_criteria.label: Reported specification and verification effort comparable to writing and testing once

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility criterion: independent teams should be able to reproduce the builds and proof checks using the disclosed artifacts and repeat the development exercise on additional representative systems. Results should report both successful cases and verification failures, along with practical limits on program size, language features, concurrency, runtime, memory and proof-search resources. A finite evaluation would establish demonstrated breadth within that envelope, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Independent reproduction and redevelopment reporting successes, failures, and practical limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed trust disclosure: enumerate the trusted checker, logic, toolchain components, instruction-set and environment models, libraries, environmental assumptions and excluded physical faults. Explain how each affects the conclusion and how difficult it is to review. Their significance should be assessed by scope and trust burden rather than simply comparing their size with the program’s line count.
completion_criteria.label: Trust-base effects and review difficulty by scope and trust burden

related_concepts.text: Roster-based distinction: SWE-02, Certified synthesis of system-scale programs from reviewable specifications, overlaps in producing an implementation with correctness evidence. SWE-01 starts with systems code supplied by developers and automates its verification and compilation; SWE-02 additionally concerns generating the implementation from a specification. Proof automation could support both, but successful verification of supplied code would not by itself demonstrate system-scale synthesis.

Roster-based distinction: SWE-03, Demonstrable adequacy of a specification against intent and the environment, concerns whether the specification asks for the right behavior. SWE-01 concerns whether an executable implements that specification. SWE-06, Sound behavioral recovery of legacy systems, concerns recovering trustworthy descriptions of existing behavior that might supply inputs to later verification. Neither proving conformance nor recovering existing behavior alone establishes that the behavior is desirable.

Roster-based distinction: SWE-04, A compositional calculus for concurrent systems that fail, could provide reasoning principles for concurrency, crashes and recovery within SWE-01’s practical envelope. SWE-08, Sequential meaning for fault-tolerant distributed execution, concerns the behavioral meaning offered by distributed execution despite failures. SWE-09, Observable determinism as the default for parallel systems code, concerns controlling externally visible variation in parallel execution. These could make particular specifications or proofs easier to express, but verifying compilation does not automatically supply any of those execution semantics.

Roster-based distinction: SWE-05, Assurance that stays proportional to each behavioral change, concerns the cost of preserving assurance as software evolves. SWE-01’s proposed initial-development cost bar does not establish that later modifications remain inexpensive. Proof reuse and repair are relevant to both, but SWE-05 is a distinct maintenance objective rather than an established prerequisite or the only possible route to sustainable evolution.

Roster-based distinction: SWE-07, Practical confinement of general untrusted programs, concerns restricting what untrusted code can do. SWE-01 concerns establishing specified functional behavior for code in a supported verification envelope. A verified confinement mechanism could enforce a boundary around unverified applications without proving those applications functionally correct.

Roster-based distinction: SWE-10, Proof-carrying behavioral composition across trust boundaries, overlaps with SWE-01’s production of executable-associated proof evidence, while adding the problem of accepting and composing behavioral guarantees from separately trusted parties. Producing a proof for one program does not automatically settle cross-party specification compatibility, composition or independent checking arrangements.

SWE-11, Proved semantics-preserving transformation of practical systems, supplies a distinct link: preserving established behavior through transformations such as compilation. CompCert illustrates this distinction. A preservation theorem can transport separately proved source properties to compiled code under its conditions, while SWE-01 additionally requires automatic establishment of the application’s functional obligations at practical cost. This relationship preserves both entries rather than treating a verified compiler implementation as the complete verifying-compilation breakthrough.

unresolved_issues: Whether any toolchain meets the complete scope, automation, executable-assurance and cost target as of 1 November 2026 remains unresolved without a bounded freshness assessment.
The seL4 FAQ’s approximate April 2025 RISC-V size and exact multicore-verification statement remain unconfirmed because its retained extraction was unreadable.
Hoare’s exact wording and bibliographic attribution, IronFleet’s reported paper-specific findings and developer burden, and the Brun roadmap characterization remain unverified in the supplied review.
The reported October 2026 proof corpus was not independently checked; the supplied article and appendix establish what was reported, not independent reproduction of every proof.

The proposed development-cost threshold still requires an operational evaluation protocol, including baseline development effort, team expertise and accounting for specification work, computation and outside assistance.
Detailed boundaries among the related concepts remain provisional because only their roster titles and limited cross-references were supplied.

brief.title: Software that comes with proof it works as specified
possible: A software team could build a database, operating-system service or networked service and receive both a runnable program and an automatically checked mathematical proof that it follows its specification: a precise statement of required behavior.

Developers without proof expertise could get this assurance with effort comparable to ordinary development. The proof would cover the executable people actually run, including recovery from crashes where the specification requires it.
why: For the behavior covered by the proof, teams could rule out violations instead of relying on tests to discover them. Strong correctness guarantees could become part of everyday software development.

Ordinary teams could gain assurance now associated with exceptional verification projects. They could spend less effort hunting for errors already excluded by proof and more effort checking requirements, interfaces and assumptions.

shown: The seL4 project has proved that supported versions of its operating-system core follow their specifications, sometimes through to the executable. CompCert proves that compilation preserves supported programs' behavior. Verus reduces proof effort for practical systems.

Anthropic and Theorem report automated no-crash proofs for selected entry points across 123 libraries. These cover restricted execution conditions and narrower properties than full required behavior. Independent reproduction remains needed.
missing: Ordinary developers still need a demonstrated way to obtain automatic proofs of rich required behavior for representative practical systems.
The same workflow must connect those proofs to the exact executable, including simultaneous operations and specified failure recovery.
A complete demonstration must account for specification work, computing cost and outside expertise at a burden comparable to ordinary development.
Independent teams must repeat the development exercise across additional systems and establish its practical limits.

milestones.label: Non-specialists produce a working executable with a checked proof
milestones.explanation: A non-specialist team would have to build a representative system with simultaneous operations and prove its executable meets an independently reviewable specification. This would establish practical use beyond expert projects.

milestones.label: Certification follows proof status for the exact executable
milestones.explanation: Certification would have to require discharged proof obligations, distinguish missing proofs from violations and state the behaviors covered for the exact executable. This would make the guarantee clear and enforceable.

milestones.label: Proof effort stays comparable to ordinary development
milestones.explanation: Additional specification and verification effort would have to be comparable to writing and testing the system once, counting computation and all assistance. This would establish affordability without hiding work elsewhere.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce results and establish practical limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to repeat builds, proof checks and development on further representative systems, reporting successes, failures and resource limits. This would establish how broadly the capability works.

milestones.label: The guarantee's trusted foundations are explicit and reviewable
milestones.explanation: The work would have to identify trusted tools, logic, libraries, execution models and excluded physical faults, explaining their effects and review difficulty. This would establish what accepting the proof requires trusting.

uncertain: The proposed cost threshold needs a fair comparison that accounts for team expertise, specification work, computing resources and outside assistance.
The practical breadth of automatic proofs across systems with simultaneous operations and failure recovery remains an open question.
A correct implementation can follow inadequate requirements; deciding whether the specification captures user intent remains a separate challenge.

page.title: Automatic verifying compilation for systems software
page.definition: A toolchain turns systems code and a formal specification, a mathematical statement of required behavior, into an executable and a machine-checked proof that it implements that behavior. Supporting invariants and proofs are generated automatically within a declared language and execution model.

goal.need: Verus’s 2024 systems case studies contain about 6,100 implementation lines and 31,000 proof lines. The first seL4 proof involved about 25 person-years for design, documentation, implementation and verification, including research and tooling. These measure proof-code volume and whole-project effort respectively; neither establishes today’s marginal verification cost. They motivate reducing the work needed to obtain functional-correctness proofs.

figures.caption: The first completed seL4 correctness proof, 2009
figures.note: The proof scripts were manually written and machine checked. These are historical project counts.

statements.body: Microsoft Research — Tony Hoare’s grand-challenge proposal
statements.quote: If the project is successful, a verifying compiler will be available as a standard tool in some widely used programming productivity toolset.
The overarching goal of PROVERS is to make formal methods accessible to non-experts
statements.context: The solicitation also calls for minimizing effects on existing development processes and performance.

completion.title: Non-specialists obtain automatically constructed functional-correctness proofs for systems binaries.
completion.criterion: A team without formal-verification specialists supplies a systems application's code and an independently reviewed functional specification. One toolchain emits a runnable binary and a machine-checkable proof that its modeled executions satisfy that specification, automatically constructing supporting invariants and proofs. Required functional behavior includes termination, concurrency and failure recovery where specified. An independent team reproduces the build and proof check. Undischarged obligations prevent certification.
completion.basis: Searches of Hoare’s grand challenge, DARPA’s PROVERS solicitation, the trusted-software roadmap, and verifying-compiler standards, prizes and benchmarks found no published test combining non-expert use, automatic functional proof construction and binary coverage. This provisional test combines those goals. Hoare’s published test permits partial verification and an unverified compiler; PROVERS supplies programme-specific usability and proof-repair targets.

milestones.title: A verifier automatically proves annotated source code satisfies its functional contracts.
milestones.criterion: An implemented verifier proves annotated source programs satisfy their functional contracts by generating verification conditions and automatically discharging them. Developers may supply loop invariants and other proof annotations. Leino and Schulte’s 2007 account describes Spec# as a prototype and gives a verifier construction for a core multithreaded language. This establishes source-level verification with supplied proof guidance.
milestones.set_by: Deductive-verification convention, described by Microsoft Research’s Leino and Schulte in A Verifying Compiler for a Multi-threaded Object-Oriented Language.
milestones.threshold_quote: A verifying compiler automatically verifies the correctness of a source program before compiling it.

milestones.title: A systems implementation has a machine-checked proof of refinement to its functional specification.
milestones.criterion: A machine-checked proof establishes that a systems implementation refines its abstract functional specification under stated assumptions. Specialist proof engineering is permitted. seL4 completed its initial C-level functional-correctness proof in 2009. Verus’s 2024 persistent-log case study establishes refinement to an abstract infinite log and atomicity with respect to crashes; its assurance trusts Verus, its solvers and the Rust compiler.
milestones.set_by: seL4 project, the functional-correctness criterion in seL4 Proofs, published for verified kernel configurations.
milestones.threshold_quote: behaves precisely as specified in the seL4 specification and nothing more.

milestones.title: A compiler has a machine-checked semantic-preservation theorem from source code to assembly.
milestones.criterion: For every supported source program successfully compiled, a machine-checked theorem establishes that generated assembly behavior improves on an allowed source behavior. CompCert proves this from CompCert C syntax trees to assembly syntax trees. Improvement permits elimination of undefined behavior; nondeterministic choices may be resolved. The theorem transports separately established source properties but does not prove application correctness, assembling or linking.
milestones.set_by: CompCert project, Semantic preservation theorem in the CompCert C manual.
milestones.threshold_quote: then the observable behavior of C improves on one of the allowed observable behaviors of S.

milestones.title: A systems binary has a machine-checked proof that it implements its functional specification.
milestones.criterion: The machine code executed by the processor is proved to implement source behavior covered by a functional-correctness theorem. seL4 reports this property for configurations supporting binary correctness. Ironclad Apps reported a related assembly-level result in 2014 for four applications and their kernel, drivers and libraries: remote clients observe outputs permitted by abstract state machines. Ironclad retained manual annotations and hardware assumptions; about 6,500 runnable implementation lines took about 3 person-years to verify.
milestones.set_by: seL4 project, the binary-correctness criterion in seL4 Proofs, published for configurations supporting that additional proof.
milestones.threshold_quote: the binary code implements precisely the behaviour of the specification, and nothing more.

milestones.title: Agents prove properties of systems machine code without human-written proof code.
milestones.criterion: Agents construct checked machine-code proofs against approved specifications without human-written proof code; expert specifications and strategy may remain. On 10 November 2026, Google DeepMind reported this for libsignal security, with about 6.5 million Lean proof lines and trusted routine contracts. On 22 October 2026, Anthropic and Theorem reported no-crash proofs for 239 entry points across 123 libraries: single-threaded static RISC-V binaries, fixed memory and inputs below 64 MiB. Both are developer reports, not peer reviewed; neither establishes a general non-expert functional-correctness workflow.
milestones.set_by: Google DeepMind, AlphaProof Code, sections 2.4 and 7; its published acceptance procedure combines approved theorem statements with Lean kernel checking.
milestones.threshold_quote: A proof is accepted only if it proves exactly the statements the user approved.

milestones.title: Non-experts prove >10 property classes with <5% residual findings and 1% manual proof changes.
milestones.criterion: Under PROVERS phase-three conditions, traditional developers work on programme-designated high-complexity systems. The published targets are more than 10 classes of system properties proved, less than 5% of serious red-team findings remaining, and 1% of proof lines requiring manual change after software updates or maintenance. These are tentative programme goals assessed through independent evaluation, rather than requirements for full functional correctness or automatic initial proof construction.
